newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Number of Austrians out of work hits new record.
newsitem.headline: Number of Austrians out of work hits new record.

text.p: Austrian unemployment soared above 300,000 for the first time in January, as construction workers flooded the market and economic growth remained sluggish.

At the end of January 301,982 people, or 9.2 percent of the workforce, were out of a job, the Social Affairs Ministry said in a statement. That was a rise of 40,989 against December and 6,441 against the previous January.
"Construction workers entered the job market later than usual this winter. That goes a long way to explaining the big rise against December," the ministry said.
It was at pains to emphasise that, based on European Union calculations, Austrian unemployment was relatively low at 4.1 percent, unchanged from December.
"Within Europe only Luxembourg is better placed," it said.

Economists agreed that Austrian unemployment was among the lowest in the industrialised world but they cautioned that sluggish economic growth coupled with belt tightening in the public sector pointed to higher joblessness for the next two years.

"This year we expect average unemployment of 245,000, which represents an increase of 15,000 against 1996," said Karl Pichelmann, employment analyst at the Vienna-based Institute for Advanced Studies (IHS).
The market would stabilise in 1998 but not before the end of the century would Austria manage to return to the employment levels of the mid-1990s, Pichelmann added.
Research institute WIFO, whose figures form the basis of government policy, also forecast a significant rise in the average number of unemployed this year, continuing a two-year trend.
Pichelmann said economic growth of just 1-1.5 percent annually had contributed to lay-offs in industry at the same time as the government attempted to rein in spending in the public sector.
"And for once the service sector, hit by increased competition, has failed to absorb the job seekers," he said.

Austria's left-right coalition government, painfully aware of how jobless rates of around 26 percent fired social unrest in 1930s, have vowed to move the battle against unemployment to the top of the political agenda.
"The fight against unemployment will be our main task in the future," Social Democrat Chancellor Viktor Klima said in his maiden speech to parliament last week.
The opposition Freedom Party, Europe's biggest far right parliamentary grouping, has scored immense political mileage by linking rising joblessness to Austria's two-year EU membership.

Pichelmann of the IHS rejected the Freedom Party's line. "Structural problems have existed for a long time and we would have gone through an even more difficult transition if we had not joined the EU," he said.
